hook: How slow would time have to be to watch light move? One kitchen second, slowed ten times, a thousand, a billion and a trillion, until light itself crawls.

Strong paradox but promises more than the film proves (light is not literally slower than a snail; at that scale it is).

winner.title: How Much Would You Slow Time to Watch Light Move?
winner.why: The title is a question people can guess at; the frame is the light front the film really delivers at a billion times slower (one second lasts about 32 years); the number on the thumbnail is not in the title. No human figure exists in the film, so the human anchor from 'What's working' is skipped.

chatgptPrompt: Create a YouTube thumbnail, 16:9 (1920x1080). Subject: a bright front of light caught halfway across a dim kitchen counter, the lit side warm and the far side in shadow, a water drop falling from a tap above a white cup. Composition: tap and cup centre, the front arcing across the counter, dark wall at upper right for text. Lighting and treatment: a single warm light front against shadow, warm wooden counter, premium editorial science documentary look, clearly a code-rendered illustration rather than a photograph. Mood: curiosity. Text: '32 YEARS' very large in cream white above 'in one second' in warm yellow, upper right. Scientific accuracy: at a billion times slower one real second lasts about 32 years and light moves about 30 centimeters per screen second. Avoid: no arrows, circles, faces, logos, watermarks, extra text. Style: distinctive, not generic AI art.
